newsitem.title: FRANCE: Mitterrand's doctor to pay damages over book.
newsitem.headline: Mitterrand's doctor to pay damages over book.

text.p: A court ordered Francois Mitterrand's doctor on Wednesday to pay damages to the late French president's relatives, and upheld a ban on the book disclosing details of his fatal cancer.

Dr Claude Gubler had already been sentenced to a four-month suspended jail term for breaching medical secrecy by revealing in a book that Mitterrand allgedly misled the French people for over a decade about the cancer which finally killed him.

The court, which heard the case on Wednesday, said Gubler should pay 340,000 francs ($68,000) to Mitterrand's relatives for invasion of privacy in his book Le Grand Secret (The Big Secret). The family had asked for 800,000 francs ($160,000).
Published a week after Mitterrand died in January, and eight months after he left office, the book was banned within 24 hours after its first print run of 40,000 copies had sold out.
In the book, Gubler said that Mitterrand, a Socialist who served two seven-year terms beginning in 1981, learned he had cancer within months of his election but kept it secret until 1992.

The court ruled that nothing had cleared the doctor of his professional obligation to medical secrecy and that his revelations after Mitterrand's death were an intolerable attack on the feelings of his family.

"Neither Gubler's desire to re-establish the truth, as he says, nor the publication during Mitterrand's lifetime of incomplete medical bulletins on his health -- which the doctor signed -- justify the revelations at issue," the ruling said.

The court ordered Gubler and his publisher Plon to pay 100,000 francs ($20,000) to Mitterrand's widow Danielle, and 80,000 francs ($16,000) to each of his three children -- Gilbert and Jean-Christophe Mitterrand, and Mazarine Pingeot.
Journalist Michel Gonod, with whom Gubler wrote the book, told reporters the ruling marked "the triumph of lies and censorship."
"This is an attack on freedom...The statue of the commander is still there, and we mustn't touch it," he said in a reference to Mozart's opera Don Giovanni.
"I'd expected something more contemporary on public awareness of politicians' private lives," Plon's lawyer Jean-Claude Zylberstein said.
Despite a pledge of openness about his health, Mitterrand issued misleading medical bulletins twice a year.

The physician testified that he wrote to set the record straight rather than for personal gain and pledged to donate any proceeds to charity after payment of his legal bills. He no longer practises medicine.

Gubler said he agreed to keep the cancer from the public -- and not to resign as the president's physician -- because he felt that Mitterrand had trapped him into lying by ordering him to treat the illness as a state secret.
The book provides details about Mitterrand's diagnoses, treatments and anxieties and argued that pain made him unfit to rule by November 1994, seven months before his term ended.
